af: The afghani has been Afghanistan's currency since the 1920s. The 1961 issues here still carry the portrait of Mohammed Zahir Shah, the last king, who reigned for four decades before the 1973 coup ended the monarchy.
dz: Algeria's 1974 5 centimes belongs to the wave of coins minted under the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's FAO coin plan — a 1970s–80s program that encouraged newly developing economies to strike low-denomination coins publicising food-security goals, which is why so many FAO-marked coins from this era share a similar civic, almost poster-like design language.
ad: Andorra has never issued its own base currency — it used French francs and Spanish pesetas side by side for most of its history and now uses the euro without being an EU member. This 1999 cèntim, minted under the FAO coin program and bearing the co-prince Joan Martí i Alanis, is a rare example of the microstate striking coinage in its own name at all.
am: The dram replaced the Soviet rouble as Armenia's currency after independence in 1991, with a full decimal coin series introduced from 1994. These pieces, spanning 5 to 500 dram, capture the young republic establishing its own monetary identity within a decade of leaving the USSR.
au: Australia decimalised its currency in 1966, replacing pounds, shillings and pence with dollars and cents. The dollar coins here trace Elizabeth II's changing official coinage portrait across more than three decades — from the 3rd portrait used into the 1990s through to the 6th portrait introduced in 2019 — alongside one-off commemoratives like the Donation Dollar, struck with a deliberately incomplete design so shopkeepers could tell it apart from ordinary change.
at: Austria's euro coins carry a national 'map' side that was updated once the EU expanded — the 2009 and 2010 pieces here use the second-generation design showing all EU member states rather than just the pre-2004 members.
az: Azerbaijan's qapik is the subunit of its manat, reintroduced after independence from the Soviet Union. This 2006 20 qapik piece belongs to the country's first fully modern decimal coin series.
bh: Bahrain's dinar is divided into 1,000 fils, one of the finer subdivisions of any modern currency. This 500 fils piece — exactly half a dinar — carries the name of King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, who has ruled since 1999.
bd: Bangladesh's taka and poisha coinage includes several FAO commemorative pieces from the 1990s, part of the same international program encouraging food-security messaging on circulating coins, alongside a 2004 2 taka marking the United Nations Literacy Decade.
bb: Barbados adopted its own dollar in 1973 after leaving the East Caribbean currency union. This 2020 dollar's flying-fish design references the national symbol that also appears on the Barbadian flag's coat of arms.
by: Belarus issued this 1 kopeck in 2009 as part of a full redesign of its rouble-denominated coinage — one of the country's first modern circulating coin series after independence, since low-value transactions had mostly been handled with banknotes through the 1990s.
be: Belgium mints its coins with parallel French and Dutch legends — reflecting the country's two main linguistic communities — which is why coins of the same denomination and year sometimes exist in visibly different text varieties, as seen in the 1977 and 1982 francs here. The collection also bridges the franc era under Kings Baudouin I and Albert II through to the first euro cents from 2000.
bz: Belize's dollar is pegged to the US dollar at a fixed 2:1 rate. This 2006 5 cents, struck in aluminium, is a lightweight low-denomination piece typical of small Commonwealth economies looking to cut coin production costs.
bt: Bhutan's ngultrum system, including the chhertum subunit, only fully modernised in the late 20th century — before that, coinage bore the king's portrait under older denominational names, as on the 1950 half rupee of the third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck.
br: These two Brazilian coins bookend a turbulent monetary period — the 1898 200 réis under the old Republic, and the 1922 1000 réis struck for the centennial of Brazil's independence from Portugal, before the réis was eventually replaced by later currencies through the 20th century.
bg: Bulgaria's stotinki coins from the 1970s–80s carry the country's second socialist-era coat of arms, used until the political changes of 1989–90 prompted a redesign of the national emblem.
bi: Burundi's franc has circulated since independence from Belgium in 1962. This 2011 50 francs is a relatively recent example of the country's small, low-relief circulating coinage.
ca: Canada is known for colourised commemorative circulation coins — a practice that turns ordinary pocket change into a limited-run collectible, as seen in the poppy-red 2014 Remembrance toonie and the coloured D-Day and Bill Reid pieces here. The 2024 Charles III issue marks the currency's transition to Canada's new monarch after Elizabeth II's seven-decade run on Canadian coinage.
cl: Chile's 2021 1 peso honours Rapa Nui (Easter Island) heritage, a reminder that the peso — reintroduced in 1975 after a period using the escudo — circulates across a territory stretching from the Andes to Polynesia.
cn: This entry spans the wider Chinese-currency sphere rather than one single mint: an 18th-century Qianlong-era cash coin from imperial China, Portuguese-administered Macau patacas (including a 1980 piece still bearing Elizabeth II as a Hong Kong-linked issue), and a long run of modern PRC yuan. The most distinctive thread is China's annual lunar zodiac commemorative series — the Year of the Monkey, Rooster, Dog, Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Snake and Horse coins here — alongside circulating pieces celebrating UNESCO-listed mountains and the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics.
co: Colombia's peso has been the national currency since the 19th century. The jump from 1 peso in 1974 to 200 pesos in 1994 reflects two decades of inflation that pushed everyday transactions toward much higher face values.
cu: Cuba's 'Patria o Muerte' ('Fatherland or Death') legend on this 2008 1 centavo is a direct piece of revolutionary-era political messaging, a phrase associated with Fidel Castro that appeared on Cuban coinage for decades after 1959.
cy: Cyprus used its own pound, divided into cents, until adopting the euro in 2008 — this collection holds one coin from each currency, either side of that changeover.
dk: Denmark's coinage bridges two long reigns: the 1929 and 1936 øre pieces carry Christian X, king through both World Wars, while the later kroner coins belong to Margrethe II, who became Europe's longest-reigning queen before her 2024 abdication.
eg: Egypt's pound and qirsh coins are struck in both standard and magnetic-material versions for different eras — the 2010 pound here is a magnetic-alloy issue, part of a broader shift many mints made toward cheaper, vending-machine-friendly metals in the 2000s.
er: Eritrea introduced the nakfa as its own currency only in 1997, after decades of using the Ethiopian birr — this 10 cents comes from that first independent coinage.
ee: Estonia's kroon, introduced in 1992 after independence from the Soviet Union, was one of the most stable currencies in the former Eastern Bloc before the country adopted the euro in 2011. This 2000 1 kroon dates from the kroon's decade as a fully independent currency.
sz: Eswatini (Swaziland at the time) issued this FAO-program 2 cents in 1975 under King Sobhuza II, whose reign of over 60 years makes him one of the longest-reigning monarchs to have appeared on circulating coinage.
fj: Fiji's coinage carried Elizabeth II's portrait from the country's earliest post-war issues — this 1965 penny predates Fiji's 1970 independence from Britain, when it was still a crown colony using British-style pre-decimal denominations.
fi: Finland's collection runs from markka-and-penni coinage used for most of the 20th century through to the first euro coins after 2000 — including two unusual non-circulating tokens, a 1960 savings-week medal and a 1962 savings-bank token, the kind of promotional pieces Nordic banks issued to encourage saving.
fr: France's franc coinage here spans nearly the whole late-20th-century run of the currency, including the Semeuse ('Sower') design signed by its original 1897 sculptor Oscar Roty, right through to the first French euro cents after 2002. The 1994 2 francs honouring Jean Moulin — a leader of the French Resistance killed by the Gestapo in 1943 — and the 1994 20 francs marking the founding of the International Olympic Committee both reflect France's habit of using commemorative coinage to mark national history.
ge: Georgia's tetri, introduced in 1993, was the country's first independent coinage after leaving the Soviet Union — this 1 tetri is a low-denomination piece from that founding series.
de: This run covers an unusually long stretch of German monetary history: an 1875 Empire pfennig, a 1901 Prussian 5 mark under Kaiser Wilhelm II, Weimar-era rentenpfennig from the 1924 currency stabilisation, West German Deutsche Mark coins through the postwar decades, and finally German euro coins from 2002 onward — including a rare 2018 1 euro cent, a denomination Germany has all but stopped striking for circulation because its production cost exceeds its face value.
gr: Greece's drachma coinage — some pieces marked with 'old lettering', later ones with reformed spelling — gave way to the euro in 2002. The 2006 20 euro cent here carries Greece's first-generation 'map' design, issued a few years after the currency switch.
gt: Guatemala's quetzal, named after the national bird, is divided into centavos. This 2009 10 centavos is struck in a magnetic alloy typical of the country's more recent low-denomination coinage.
gn: Guinea's franc has been the national currency since independence from France in 1958. This 1987 25 francs guinéens dates from a currency reform decade after a brief, ill-fated experiment with a different unit, the syli.
hu: Hungary's forint coinage bridges the late socialist period and the post-1989 republic; the 2020 20 forint marking 'tribute to the heroes' is part of Hungary's ongoing practice of using low-denomination circulation coins for historical commemoration, a role most countries reserve for higher-value or non-circulating pieces.
in: The largest holding in the cabinet, and the only one that needs eight separate drawers. It opens with a copper massa struck under Rajaraja I of the Chola dynasty a thousand years ago, then splits between the princely states — Hyderabad, Gwalior, Indore, Jaipur, Junagadh — that struck their own coinage right up to accession in 1948, and British India, whose rupee circulated alongside them.

After 1947 the anna-and-pice system gave way to decimal 'naye paise' in 1957. From the 1970s onward the Republic leaned heavily on FAO issues and on commemorative 2-, 5- and 10-rupee pieces marking everything from Independence anniversaries to national institutions — a habit that continues in the 75-years-of-Independence coins struck this decade.
id: Indonesia's rupiah has been in continuous use since independence from the Netherlands. The jump from a 1952 1 sen to a 1999 50 rupiah reflects decades of inflation that eventually made the sen — one-hundredth of a rupiah — worthless enough to disappear entirely from circulation.
iq: Iraq's 1975 5 fils, struck under the FAO coin program, predates the decades of conflict and currency instability that would later reshape Iraqi coinage entirely — this is a rare surviving low-denomination piece from a more settled monetary era.
ie: Ireland's pre-euro punt coinage (the 1999 20 pence here) used the same denominations as British coinage of the era despite being fully independent currency, before Ireland became one of the original 1999–2002 adopters of the euro.
il: Israel's coinage moved from the lira (the 1975 1 lira here) to the new agora system in the late 1970s as the country battled severe inflation — the 1977 and 1987 10 agorot pieces belong to that reformed currency, itself eventually replaced again by the modern new shekel in 1985.
it: Italy's 500 lire and euro coins bookend the currency switch of 2002. The 500 lire pairs a bronzital centre — an aluminium-bronze alloy — inside a ring of acmonital, the stainless steel the Italian mint developed for coinage. Two-metal construction was still rare in circulating money when Italy adopted it, and the same centre-and-ring approach was later carried into the €1 and €2.
jm: Jamaica's dollar coinage includes an unusual heptagonal (seven-sided) 1 dollar from 2006 — a non-round shape some Commonwealth mints use so coins can be told apart by touch, a feature especially useful for lower-value denominations handled quickly in daily transactions.
jp: This run stretches from an Edo-period 'Kan'ei Tsūhō' cash coin — cast, not struck, with the square center hole traditional to East Asian coinage for centuries — through to modern yen dated by Japan's imperial era names: Shōwa (Emperor Hirohito's reign) and Heisei (Emperor Akihito's, beginning 1989).
jo: Jordan's dinar coinage carries the portraits of its two most recent kings — Hussein, who reigned for nearly half a century until 1999, and his son Abdullah II, seen here on a 2012 quarter dinar.
kw: Kuwait's fils coinage moved to non-magnetic alloys in the late 1970s and 1980s, as seen in both pieces here — a material choice many Gulf states made to keep coins from corroding in humid, coastal conditions.
lr: Liberia's dollar coinage ranges from a conventional 1937 2 cents to a distinctly unconventional 1995 commemorative 1 dollar featuring Captain Kirk and Captain Picard from Star Trek — Liberia has long used novelty and pop-culture commemoratives, minted for the international collector market rather than everyday transactions, to generate revenue.
lt: Lithuania adopted the euro in 2015 — both coins here are 1 euro pieces from that first year, part of the country's final currency changeover in the Baltic states' staggered path from national currencies to the euro.
lu: Luxembourg's 1930 10 centimes carries Grand Duchess Charlotte, who reigned for 45 years and led the country's government-in-exile during the Second World War — one of the longer monarchical tenures reflected anywhere in this collection.
mg: Madagascar's franc coinage continued under French colonial administration until independence in 1960; this 1953 5 francs predates that transition by seven years.
mw: Malawi's kwacha, meaning 'dawn' in Chichewa, has been the national currency since 1971. This 2004 1 kwacha is typical of the country's modest, low-relief circulating coinage.
mr: Mauritania's ouguiya is one of the few currencies in the world historically subdivided on a base-5 system rather than the usual decimal 100, a legacy of its 1973 introduction as a distinct Islamic-compliant alternative to the French-linked CFA franc used by its neighbours.
mu: Mauritius's rupee coinage moved from Elizabeth II's early colonial-era portrait on the 1978 1 rupee to fully independent republican designs by the 1990s, tracking the island nation's 1968 transition from British colony to independent Commonwealth member.
na: Namibia introduced its own dollar in 1993, three years after independence from South Africa. This 2000 5 cents, struck under the FAO program, is from the currency's first full decade.
np: Nepal's coinage is dated using the Bikram Sambat calendar and, until 2008, always carried the reigning monarch's portrait — tracing Prithvi Bir Bikram through Tribhuvan, Mahendra, Birendra and Gyanendra. The 2007 and 2009 rupees, both explicitly marked 'Monarchy/Republic', capture the exact moment Nepal abolished its 240-year-old monarchy in 2008 and became a federal republic.
nl: The Netherlands' guilder coinage here runs through three reigns — Wilhelmina, Juliana and Beatrix — before the 2002 euro switch, with a 2025 colourised 50 cent added as a modern reminder that the Netherlands still issues commemorative pieces even now within the eurozone.
nz: New Zealand's 2006 20 and 50 cent pieces belong to a broader Commonwealth-wide coin redesign of that decade, when several countries moved their smaller denominations to cheaper magnetic-steel alloys — hence both being marked 'Magnetic' here.
mk: North Macedonia's denar coinage began after independence from Yugoslavia in 1991; the 1993 50 deni predates the country's full modern decimal series, which the 2008 denari pieces here represent.
no: Norway's kroner coinage spans two kings: Olav V, seen across most of these pieces from 1969 through his death in 1991, and his son Harald V from 1995 onward. The plain, low-relief 'Type 1' and 'Type 2' 5 kroner design changes reflect a subtle 1970s retooling of the coin's portrait engraving.
pk: Pakistan inherited British India's anna-based coinage at independence in 1947 before decimalising into rupees — the 1951 1 anna here predates that reform. From the 2000s onward, Pakistani commemorative rupee coins increasingly honoured individual public figures (Benazir Bhutto, Abdul Sattar Edhi, Dr. Ruth Pfau) and bilateral relationships, a shift toward using circulating coinage as a form of civic memorial.
pa: Panama's balboa is pegged 1:1 to the US dollar and Panama has never printed its own paper currency, relying on US notes — but it does strike its own coins, like this 1962 5 centésimos, to the same size and specification as US coins of equivalent value.
pg: Papua New Guinea's kina coinage tracks the country's constitutional transition from Elizabeth II, on the 2004 and 2008 pieces, to Charles III on the 2025 50 toea marking 50 years of independence from Australia.
ph: The Philippine peso's 'piso' coinage moved through several redesigns between the 1999 and 2020 coins here, including a shift to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas's updated seal — a reminder that Philippine coin design has been revised more frequently than most Southeast Asian neighbours' currencies.
pl: Poland's zloty underwent a dramatic 1995 redenomination that struck four zeroes from the currency — visible directly in this collection's jump from a 1989 20 zlotys (old currency, worth a small fraction of a US cent by the end of communist-era inflation) to a 2003 2 zlotys (new currency, worth roughly 50 cents). The post-reform 2 zloty coin became Poland's preferred canvas for commemoratives, seen here honouring Pope John Paul II, historic battles, wildlife and regional heritage.
pt: Portugal's escudo coinage from the late 1980s, seen in all four pieces here, predates the country's 2002 changeover to the euro — the escudo itself had been Portugal's currency since the fall of the monarchy in 1910.
ru: This run crosses one of the sharpest currency discontinuities in the collection: Soviet-era kopecks and roubles from 1957–1989, the chaotic dual 1993 rouble issue (both magnetic and non-magnetic versions were struck the same year during the changeover from Soviet to Russian coinage), and post-1998 Russian Federation roubles after a redenomination stripped three zeroes from the currency — explaining the jump from '50 Roubles' in 1993 to '5 Roubles' in 2018 for what is, in real terms, a much higher-value coin.
rw: Rwanda's franc coinage includes a 1970 2 francs struck under the FAO program, from well before the country's currency and coinage were affected by the upheavals of the 1990s.
sm: San Marino, one of the world's smallest republics, has long minted its own coinage despite being entirely surrounded by Italy — this 1974 10 lire, struck under the FAO program with a honeybee motif, matched the Italian lira in value and specification even though San Marino used its own designs.
sa: Saudi Arabia's riyal and halalah coinage carries the portraits of two kings here — Fahd, who reigned until 2005, and his half-brother Salman, on the country's more recent 2016 issues.
rs: Serbia's dinar coinage frequently honours cultural figures — this 2011 20 dinara depicts Ivo Andrić, the Bosnian-Serb novelist and Nobel laureate, on a coin issued the same year Serbia was formally recognised as an EU candidate country.
sl: Sierra Leone's leone, introduced in 1964, replaced British West African currency after independence — this 1987 1 leone belongs to the country's first few decades as an independent currency issuer.
sg: Singapore's cents coinage, spanning 1967 to 1996, tracks nearly three decades of a currency that has stayed remarkably stable relative to many of its regional neighbours — the ribbon motif on the reverse was even flipped between 'upwards' and 'downwards' orientations across different mintages, a small design variation collectors specifically track.
so: Somalia's 1976 10 senti, struck under the FAO program, dates from before the collapse of central government in the early 1990s that would later make Somali coinage far scarcer and more irregular.
za: South Africa's 5 cents, marked 'Suid-Afrika' (Afrikaans for South Africa) alongside its English name, reflects the country's practice of rotating which of its 11 official languages appears on a given year's coinage.
kr: South Korea's won coinage was fully re-established after the 1953 armistice and currency reform; these three pieces, spanning 1991 to 2003, represent the modern decimal won system that has remained essentially unchanged in design for decades.
es: Spain's peseta coinage here runs from Francisco Franco's final years as head of state through the full reign of Juan Carlos I, who oversaw Spain's transition to democracy after 1975 — before the currency gave way to the euro, with Spain's first- and second-generation euro map designs both represented in the later coins.
lk: Sri Lanka's coinage — still marked Ceylon under British colonial administration on the earliest pieces here — carries George V and George VI before independence in 1948, with the 1998 10 rupees marking the 50th anniversary of that independence.
se: Sweden's öre and kronor coinage spans two kings, Gustaf VI Adolf and his grandson Carl XVI Gustaf, who acceded in 1973 — Sweden abolished the öre entirely in 2010, making these low-denomination pieces a snapshot of a subunit that no longer exists.
ch: Swiss coinage is built around two designs that have barely moved in over a century: the standing figure of Helvetia on the franc pieces, and the smaller 'Libertas' head on the rappen. A 1958 20 rappen and a 2009 one are near-identical — a continuity almost no other mint has kept. Switzerland has never adopted the euro despite being ringed by the eurozone.
sy: Syria's 1979 pound and qirsh coins, all sharing the same three-star shield motif, date from the Ba'athist-era Syrian Arab Republic well before the coinage and currency became far scarcer amid the conflict that began in 2011.
tw: Taiwan's New Taiwan dollar coinage, represented here by 2006 and 2011 pieces, has remained one of the more stable East Asian currencies since its introduction in 1949, when the Republic of China government relocated to the island.
th: Thailand's baht coinage spans three kings — Rama V/VI/VIII era satang from 1937, Rama IX (Bhumibol Adulyadej, who reigned for 70 years until 2016), and Rama X's first-portrait coinage from 2018 — making the currency's royal portraiture one of the most continuous in the world.
gm: The Gambia's 1974 1 butut, struck under the FAO program, is one of the smallest subunits represented in this collection — 100 bututs make one dalasi.
tl: Timor-Leste's centavo coinage dates from shortly after the country's 2002 independence — as one of the world's newest nations, it uses centavo coins alongside the US dollar as its base currency, a dual-currency arrangement shared with only a handful of small economies.
tn: Tunisia's dinar and millime coinage moved to non-magnetic alloys by 1960, as marked on the earlier coin here, while the 1997 half dinar represents the country's more recent decimal series.
tr: Turkey's lira was redenominated in 2005, dropping six zeroes from a currency that had been battered by decades of inflation — this 2014 'heavy type' 1 lira belongs to the stable, post-reform currency rather than the old lira that briefly required million- and billion-lira banknotes.
ae: The United Arab Emirates' dirham coinage moved from a 'large type' 1984 1 dirham to smaller, non-magnetic and eventually magnetic versions of the same denomination by the 2010s — a size and material downsizing common across Gulf coinages as production costs were reconsidered.
gb: The second-largest holding, running from a Victorian threepence through six monarchs. It traces decimalisation in 1971 — when 'New Pence' briefly distinguished reformed coins from the old pounds-shillings-pence — the four-nations round pound introduced in 1983, and the full sequence of Elizabeth II's five coinage portraits.

Gibraltar sits in its own drawer here. It is a British Overseas Territory, not part of the United Kingdom, and issues its own pound at parity with sterling — which is why its coins carry Gibraltar's own reverses rather than the Royal Mint's.
us: Almost the whole of this drawer is one denomination. The quarter has carried a rotating reverse since 1999 — the 50 State Quarters, then the District of Columbia and territories, then America the Beautiful national parks, and since 2022 the American Women series, seen here in the Maya Angelou, Wilma Mankiller, Bessie Coleman, Eleanor Roosevelt and Pauli Murray issues.

The two 2010 dollars honouring Fillmore and Lincoln belong to the Presidential $1 Coin Program, which struck four new presidential portraits a year until it was cut short in 2016 with unsold coins piling up in Federal Reserve vaults.
uz: Uzbekistan's 1994 3 tiyin belongs to the country's first independent coinage, introduced the same year as its full break from the rouble zone that Central Asian republics had continued using for two years after the Soviet collapse.
ye: Yemen's coinage bridges two very different currencies — a 1976 rial from the pre-unification Yemen Arab Republic, and a 2003 10 rials from the unified Republic of Yemen formed in 1990, whose currency inherited the rial name but a completely different value scale.
zm: Zambia's kwacha coinage was redenominated in 2013, dropping three zeroes — the jump from 50 ngwee in 1992 to 1 kwacha in 2015 spans that reform, with 100 ngwee making one kwacha both before and after.
zw: Zimbabwe's 1997 2 dollars predates the hyperinflation of the 2000s that would eventually force the country to abandon its own currency altogether in 2009 in favour of foreign currencies — making this a snapshot of the Zimbabwean dollar while it still functioned as ordinary, stable pocket change.
british-crown-dependencies: Both coins here are specifically Manx — from the Isle of Man, which mints its own coinage pegged 1:1 to sterling despite not being part of the UK. The triskelion (the three-legged emblem on the 1992 10 pence) and Tynwald Hill (the ancient open-air meeting site of the Manx parliament, on the 2012 pound) are two of the island's most distinctive national symbols.
british-west-africa: This 1935 tenth-penny, bearing George V, was struck for circulation across British-administered Nigeria, the Gold Coast (now Ghana), Sierra Leone and the Gambia — a shared colonial currency issued by the West African Currency Board rather than by any individual territory.
central-african-states: This 1962 25 CFA francs was struck just two years after most of the region's constituent countries — Cameroon, Chad, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic — gained independence from France in 1960, making it an early issue of the currency union that still operates today.
east-africa: These George V and George VI pieces, from 1936 and 1952, were struck by the East African Currency Board for circulation across Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika and Zanzibar under British administration — a single coinage shared across territories that would later become separate independent nations.
french-indochina: Both 20 cent pieces date from the Second World War, when French Indochina's coinage and administration were caught between Vichy France and Japanese occupation — the 1941 issue in a distinctive non-magnetic alloy, reflecting wartime metal shortages that regularly forced mints to substitute materials.
french-west-africa: This 1944 1 franc was struck during the Second World War for France's West African colonies, a shared currency issued well before the individual territories — including Senegal, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire — gained independence in 1960.
west-african-states: This 2010 25 CFA francs, issued under the FAO coin program, represents the currency union's modern, ongoing form — the West African CFA franc still circulates today across eight countries and is pegged to the euro.
yugoslavia: This run of dinara and para coins, from 1976 to 1993, ends in the middle of Yugoslavia's catastrophic early-1990s hyperinflation — the collection holds three separate 1993 denominations (10, 50 and 100 dinara) from a single year, as the currency was repeatedly redenominated within months to keep pace with prices collapsing toward worthlessness.
